title: GenAI 101
description: A practical first path through generative AI, ChatGPT, everyday prompting and context design for AI practitioners.

chapters.title: GenAI for everyone: no jargon
chapters.summary: A friendly starting point: what generative AI does, where it helps, and why fluent answers still need checking.

sections.title: The short version
sections.body: Generative AI models learn statistical patterns from large collections of examples and use those patterns to create a likely continuation: text, code, images, audio, or other supported media. A language model is not a search index or a person with reliable understanding. It can explain and transform information impressively while still producing a confident mistake.

sections.title: A useful mental model
sections.body: Think of a capable drafting and reasoning assistant that responds to the material and instructions you provide. It can summarize, brainstorm, classify, translate, explain, and help write code. Some products add search, files, data analysis, image understanding, or other tools; availability varies by product, plan, region, workspace and current settings.

sections.title: Where humans stay in the loop
sections.body: Use AI for a first draft, options, or a faster route through material. Check important facts against trustworthy sources, test code, and apply domain judgment before acting. Avoid placing sensitive information into a tool unless its data controls and your organization’s rules permit it. NIST’s risk profile is a useful reminder to consider privacy, information integrity, bias, security and downstream impact throughout a system’s life.

sections.title: Try this today
sections.body: Choose a low-risk task you already understand. Ask for a summary, rewrite or list of alternatives. Compare the result with your own knowledge, identify one weak spot, and request a targeted revision. The aim is learning where the tool helps, not handing over responsibility.

chapters.code:
Useful task: Turn these meeting notes into a 5-bullet recap for a busy teammate. Keep decisions separate from open questions. If a detail is missing, mark it as unknown rather than guessing.

[Paste only material you are allowed to share.]
apply: Name one repetitive task where a draft would save time.
Use a low-risk example you can independently verify.
Treat unsupported or high-impact claims as questions to check.
Check which tools and controls are actually available in your account.
Decide what information policy allows before sharing it.

chapters.title: Your ChatGPT journey: first task to steady workflow
chapters.summary: A repeatable path from a first question to a checked result, with product features treated as optional tools rather than assumptions.

sections.title: 1. Start with a real task
sections.body: Pick a concrete job: understand a document, draft a reply, compare options, or plan a project. Say what a useful result would let you do. You do not need special prompt jargon to begin.

sections.title: 2. Give it the working material
sections.body: State relevant background, audience, constraints and format. If your ChatGPT experience offers file upload, search, data analysis or other tools, use them when the task benefits. Capabilities, limits and interface labels can vary with plan, region, workspace and product updates, so follow the controls shown in your account.

sections.title: 3. Iterate like a conversation
sections.body: Read the answer as a draft. Point out what is missing, correct a mistaken assumption, or ask for a different level of detail. Ask the system to distinguish evidence from uncertainty when the distinction matters. For current facts, use an available search feature and open the cited sources yourself.

sections.title: 4. Check, keep and reuse
sections.body: Verify consequential facts and test any suggested code or calculations. For recurring work, projects can help keep related chats and files together where that feature is available. Review your account’s data controls and follow workplace policy before adding confidential material; chat history, memory and model-improvement settings are separate choices.

chapters.code:
I need to [task] for [audience].
Relevant context: [facts or source material].
Please return [format] with [constraints].
If information is missing, ask me or label the uncertainty.
I will check the result against [source, test, or decision rule].
apply: Choose a task and state the decision or deliverable it supports.
Supply only relevant context you are permitted to share.
Use tools or uploads only when available and useful for the task.
Iterate once with a specific correction or refinement.
Verify important output and review the account’s data controls.

chapters.title: Prompting for everyday users
chapters.summary: Plain-language instructions beat magic phrases. A small checklist makes everyday requests clearer and easier to review.

sections.title: A simple prompt recipe
sections.body: Try Task + Context + Audience + Constraints + Output. Describe the job, provide only the background that matters, name who will use the result, add boundaries, and request a shape such as a table or short email. Not every prompt needs all five parts. Start with the smallest clear request and add detail where the answer needs it.

sections.title: From vague to workable
sections.body: Vague: “Write about our launch.” Workable: “Draft a 120-word launch note for existing customers. The release adds saved filters to the dashboard. Use a warm, direct tone, avoid promises about future features, and finish with a link placeholder.” The improved version states the task, facts, audience, length, tone and boundary.

sections.title: Refine with evidence
sections.body: If the output is off, say what to change: shorten the opening, keep the original terminology, or separate facts from recommendations. Paste a sample when style matters. For facts, point to source material and ask for claims to be tied to it. Role-play labels can guide tone, but they do not grant expertise or guarantee correctness.

sections.title: Keep the request safe and reviewable
sections.body: Remove personal or confidential details unless the service and your policies allow them. Ask the model to leave unknown fields blank instead of inventing them. Before sharing the result, check names, dates, numbers, quotations and any claim that could affect someone’s rights, money or safety.

chapters.code:
Task: Draft a [kind of output].
Context: [relevant facts or pasted source].
Audience: [who will read/use it].
Constraints: [length, tone, must-include or must-avoid].
Output: [bullets, table, email, steps].
If a required fact is absent, flag it instead of making it up.
apply: Turn the request into a clear action verb.
Add audience and relevant facts; omit unrelated history.
Set only the constraints that matter for success.

Revise by naming a concrete change, then check the result.

chapters.title: Context engineering for AI practitioners
chapters.summary: Move beyond one prompt: curate the right instructions, evidence, history and tools for the model’s next step.

sections.title: Prompt versus context
sections.body: A prompt is often the instruction or message you write. Context engineering is a broader practitioner term for selecting and maintaining the information an AI system receives across a task or workflow. The term is still evolving; teams use it at different levels of detail. Context can include system instructions, the current request, retrieved documents, conversation history, tool definitions and results, application state, and output constraints.

sections.title: Context is a limited working set
sections.body: A model’s context window is the input and output material it can consider in one request, subject to the product’s implementation. Long histories, large files and tool results can crowd out the current goal or relevant evidence. Bigger is not automatically better: retrieve the smallest trustworthy set that helps the next step, label its source and date, and summarize or discard stale material.

sections.title: Design for a workflow, not a heroic prompt
sections.body: For a multi-step agent, decide what stays fixed (policy and tool rules), what changes (task and evidence), what the system may read or do, and what it must return. Carry forward compact state such as decisions and unresolved questions instead of replaying every transcript. Make tool permissions explicit and validate results at each action boundary.

sections.title: Treat retrieved text as data
sections.body: Files, web pages and tool output may contain misleading or hostile instructions. Preserve provenance, distinguish trusted policy from untrusted content, and do not let retrieved text silently override application rules. Ask for citations or structured evidence where useful, then check that the cited material supports the claim. NIST’s generative-AI risk guidance can inform a broader review of privacy, security and information integrity.

chapters.code:
Next-step context
- Goal: [current objective]
- Trusted instructions: [stable rules and allowed tools]
- Relevant evidence: [source, date, excerpt]
- Decisions already made: [short state]
- Open questions: [unknowns]
- Action boundary: [what requires approval or validation]
- Output contract: [schema or expected result]

Exclude stale history and treat retrieved instructions as untrusted data.
apply: Separate stable policy from the current task and retrieved evidence.
